content: Zinc oxide is a chemical compound with the formula ZnO. It is nearly insoluble in water but dissolves in acids and alkalis. It appears as white hexagonal crystals or a white powder, commonly referred to as zinc white. When exposed to hydrogen sulfide or ultraviolet light, it retains its white color. Crystalline zinc oxide exhibits piezoelectric properties and is thermochromic, meaning it changes color from white to yellow when heated and reverts to white upon cooling. At approximately 1975°C, zinc oxide decomposes into zinc vapor and oxygen. High-quality single-crystalline ZnO is almost transparent. In nature, zinc oxide occurs as the mineral zincite. Medical Applications Zinc oxide lozenges are a popular over-the-counter remedy for colds, but numerous studies have failed to demonstrate significant efficacy. A mixture containing 5% iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃), known as calamine, is used in calamine lotion. Historically, the minerals zincite and hemimorphite have also been referred to as calamine. When combined with eugenol, zinc oxide forms a material with restorative and prosthodontic applications in dentistry. Zinc peroxide (ZnO₂·½H₂O) is a white to yellow powder used in antiseptic ointments. As a Pigment Zinc white is used as a pigment in paints. It is more opaque than lithopone but less opaque than titanium dioxide. It is also used in coatings for paper. A special grade of zinc white, known as Chinese white, is used in artists' pigments. Zinc oxide absorbs both UVA and UVB rays of ultraviolet light, making it a key ingredient in ointments, creams, and lotions for sunburn protection and skin damage prevention. It is the broadest-spectrum UVA and UVB absorber approved by the FDA for use in sunscreens and is completely photostable. Additionally, due to its antimicrobial and antifungal properties, zinc oxide is the primary active ingredient recommended by pediatricians for treating diaper rash. Rubber Manufacture Zinc oxide, combined with stearic acid, is used in the commercial production of rubber goods. This mixture facilitates faster and more controllable rubber curing. Zinc oxide can also serve as a filler in certain rubber mixtures. Thin Film and Semiconductor Applications Zinc oxide is widely used in thin-film technology, particularly in laser diodes and light-emitting diodes (LEDs), due to its exciton and biexciton energies of 60 meV and 15 meV, respectively. These properties are expected to improve further with epitaxy. N-type doped films of zinc oxide, achieved by introducing aluminum, indium, or excess zinc, are commonly used as transparent conducting oxides (TCOs). Oxygen vacancies in ZnO increase conductivity by generating states in the band gap. P-type doping, however, remains challenging and is an active area of research, with arsenic being a leading candidate dopant. Applications include thin-film solar cells, LCDs, and flat-panel displays. Appropriately doped ZnO can be both transparent and conductive, making it suitable as a transparent electrode. Indium tin oxide (ITO) is another transparent conducting oxide often used in microelectronics. Zinc oxide has also been considered for spintronics applications due to theoretical predictions of room-temperature ferromagnetism, though reports of ferromagnetism remain unsubstantiated. ZnO layers are typically deposited using sputter deposition or chemical vapor deposition (CVD). The latter method allows for the growth of rough layers that scatter incoming light, enhancing the efficiency of solar cells. Zinc oxide has also been observed to act as a chemical reagent in Friedel-Crafts acylation reactions. Production Methods Zinc oxide is produced primarily through two processes: 1. French Process: Metallic zinc is melted in a graphite crucible and vaporized at temperatures above 907°C. The zinc vapor reacts with oxygen in the air to form ZnO, accompanied by a drop in temperature and bright luminescence. The resulting zinc oxide particles are transported into a cooling duct and collected in a bag house. This indirect method, known as the French process, was popularized by LeClaire in France in 1844. Most of the world's zinc oxide is manufactured via this process, with major applications in industries such as rubber, varistors, sunscreens, paints, healthcare, and poultry nutrients. Recent advancements include the synthesis of acicular nanostructures (rods, wires, tripods, tetrapods, plates) using a modified French process called the catalyst-free combust-oxidized mesh (CFCOM) process. These nanostructures typically have micrometer-length nanorods with nanometric diameters (below 100 nm). 2. American Process: In this process, zinc ore (zinc ash) is dissolved as ZnCl₂ and precipitated with alkali. The resulting zinc oxide is referred to as Active Zinc Oxide. Safety Zinc oxide fumes are generated during the melting of brass, as the melting point of brass is close to the boiling point of zinc. Exposure to zinc oxide fumes in the air, such as during welding, can lead to a condition known as metal fume fever, a nervous system disorder.
